source.title: Toward Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Walter Nelson; Theofanis Karaletsos; Francesco Locatello

page_placements.theme: Encoder, dictionary and code constraints affect reconstruction

record.tranche_reason: It compares SAE design and training variants using reconstruction MSE, which bears on whether reconstruction error changes with SAE architecture. It does not analyze the error structure or test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported reconstruction MSE values are retained as evidence about error magnitude under different SAE variants. The paper does not report linear predictability of the error, per-token error norms, cross-size token overlap, or a decomposition into kinds of error.
record.test_reason: The paper is about SAE identifiability, not dark matter. Its tables still report reconstruction MSE for architecture variants (AbsTopK, aRIP-regularized iSAE, multistep-encoder iSAE-ME) against TopK on Pythia-160M and DINOv2 activations. That bears on one part of V6: whether SAE error shrinks with better architectures. The evidence is incidental, from aggregate MSE only, with no analysis of the error's structure or source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that TopK SAEs are not reliably identifiable, and that bidirectional features, aRIP regularization and a multistep encoder improve stability. They report that AbsTopK worsens reconstruction on real activations, while iSAE-ME gives the lowest LLM reconstruction error. They hypothesize that optimization, possibly also capacity, explains the remaining real-world stability gap. Their claim of a "massive reduction" in reconstruction error holds on synthetic data; on Pythia-160M the reduction is about 11%.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares TopK, AbsTopK, aRIP-regularized iSAE, and multistep-encoder iSAE-ME using reconstruction and identifiability metrics. It does not use the original study's dark-matter error-prediction or cross-size context-overlap measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reconstruction MSE varies across SAE variants and data settings: some alternatives improve on TopK, while AbsTopK and iSAE worsen MSE on Pythia-160M.

fits_no_version.finding: On noiseless synthetic data from a known dictionary, the expressive multistep encoder (iSAE-ME) drives reconstruction MSE close to zero (0.447 to 0.001 i.i.d.; 0.357 to 0.040 mixture).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When data are exactly sparse-linear, SAE reconstruction error is largely an encoder-expressiveness artifact removable by amortized-inference improvements.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The reported MSE is an aggregate reconstruction metric and does not characterize error vectors or per-token errors. The paper does not compare SAE reconstruction against random errors of matched size, does not sweep SAE sizes, and does not report uncertainty for the MSE values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 CE Loss values were not extracted as V3 results: the table reports SAE downstream loss but gives no random-error comparison of the same size. Other SAEBench metrics do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no linear prediction of the error vector from the input.
All: no per-token error norms, no SAE size sweep, no cross-size context overlap.
All: the CE loss in Table 3 has no random-error comparison of matched size.
All: no decomposition of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
All: no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.

Untested parts: the roles of the sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents and the training objective; end-to-end training; whether the remaining error reflects model representation structure; scaling of SAE size.

missing.what: SAEBench CE loss on Pythia-160M: TopK 3.974, AbsTopK 4.004, iSAE 4.003, iSAE-ME 3.906. This is a downstream-loss counterpart to the MSE rows for V6. No clean-model loss or random-error baseline is given, so it cannot support V3.

record.verdict_notes: The paper never mentions dark matter and does not cite the original. The synthetic rows are unlinked because the residual there is an artifact by construction and involves no model representation. On real activations, the error reductions are modest and mixed by variant, and no uncertainty is reported. Each setting uses a single SAE size (4096 latents, k=40), so scale effects are untested.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the SAE error vector is a linear function of the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap of contexts where larger and smaller SAEs fail, and whether error persists with scale.
Whether replacing activations with SAE reconstructions harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear and nonlinear error components differ in content or learnability.
Whether analyses of circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

The study compares reconstruction error across SAE variants, but does not test whether dark matter mostly arises from sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, or objective choice; whether end-to-end training removes it; or whether the residual's structure reflects the model representation.

relation.reason: Table 2 tests whether architecture changes reduce SAE reconstruction error. It does not test the majority causal attribution or exclusion of representation structure.

tranche.reason: The real-activation architecture comparisons provide results on V6's reconstruction-reduction component in Pythia-160M and DINOv2 settings.

source_check.notes: Section 4.1 says AbsTopK worsens reconstruction in both real models, contradicting Table 2's DINOv2 reduction. Matched training controls and SAEBench downstream evaluations are present despite the header flags; MSE uncertainty is not reported.

statements.correction: Sections 4–5 compare reconstruction and identifiability. No quantitative partition of reconstruction error into training artifacts and representation structure is reported.
statements.problem: The causal attribution is untested, but this paper does not explicitly discuss leaving dark-matter attribution open. Its concluding optimization/capacity hypothesis concerns imperfect code stability.

statements.correction: Architecture comparisons establish sensitivity of reconstruction MSE. The study does not separate training-induced error from representation structure; its remaining-gap discussion concerns code stability.
statements.problem: The lack of causal exclusion is correctly identified, but this study does not explicitly analyze the structure or causal attribution of remaining reconstruction error.
